$comment: WORKED EXAMPLE (fictional resident) so a plugged-in AI can see what 'done' looks like. Everything here was produced by running the pipeline on two short recordings. Note the artifacts: each one states what it IS, what it is NOT, and WHY it was made.

artifacts.generation_prompt: Warm illustration, 1950s small-town drugstore soda counter at dusk, teenage girl behind the counter, regulars on stools, golden light through big windows. Painterly, nostalgic. NOT photorealism; no real people depicted.
artifacts.label: Illustration inspired by 'The drugstore on 5th' — not a photograph, not the actual store.
artifacts.why: The family wanted something visual to hang beside the quote card in the gallery. A painterly illustration of the soda-counter era gives the feeling of the memory without pretending to be it.

artifacts.generation_prompt: Gentle acoustic song, 1960s folk-ballad feel, fingerpicked guitar and soft female vocal, warm and unhurried, about a mother's Sunday kitchen and a recipe that was never written down. Tender, not sad.
artifacts.label: Song inspired by 'The meal I still think about' — an original composition, not a recording of the elder, not a historical document.
artifacts.why: Margaret's daughter said her mother used to hum while cooking. A short song in that spirit gives the grandchildren something to play that carries the feeling of those Sundays — the story even names the absence (no written recipe), so music fills a gap words can't.

digests.letter: This week Margaret recorded two stories: her first job at the drugstore on 5th, and her mother's Sunday pot roast. Best line: 'People don't come here for the prescriptions. They come because somebody knows their name.' Next week: a question about her wedding day.

gallery.title: Margaret H. — a life, so far

quote_cards.context: Her boss Mr. Abernathy's advice, age 16
quote_cards.quote: People don't come here for the prescriptions. They come because somebody knows their name.

quote_cards.context: On her mother's Sunday pot roast
quote_cards.quote: She never wrote the recipe down. I've tried, God knows I've tried, and it's never right.

stories.clean_transcript: I was sixteen and Mr. Abernathy hired me at the drugstore on 5th. He said, 'Margaret, people don't come here for the prescriptions. They come because somebody knows their name.' I never forgot that. I worked that counter for four years, through high school.
stories.question: What was your first real job, and what did it teach you that school didn't?
stories.summary: At sixteen, Margaret worked the counter at Abernathy's drugstore on 5th Street. Her boss taught her that people come for being known, not for the product — a lesson she carried for life.
stories.title: The drugstore on 5th

stories.clean_transcript: My mother's pot roast. Sundays. The whole house smelled like it by noon, and my father would come in from the garage just to stand in the kitchen. She never wrote the recipe down. I've tried, God knows I've tried, and it's never right.
stories.question: What meal, made by whom, do you still think about?
stories.summary: Margaret's mother made pot roast every Sunday; the smell filled the house. No recipe was ever written down, and Margaret has never been able to recreate it.
stories.title: The meal I still think about

suggested_questions: You mentioned your mother several times but we have no story about her directly — would you tell us about her as a young woman?
What happened to Abernathy's drugstore? When did you last see Mr. Abernathy?
You worked that counter through high school — what came after graduation?
